hints: Focus on what it means for sulfuric acid to be an oxidising agent here, it must oxidise the halide ion to the halogen while itself being reduced to sulfur products.
Recall the first reaction with NaCl gives only steamy white fumes of HCl with no colour change, so no oxidation happens there.
Remember that bromide and iodide are stronger reducing agents than chloride, so think about which ones go further to give brown Br2 fumes and purple I2 fumes plus SO2.
walkthrough:
**Start with what oxidising agent means**

Think side by side with me. If sulfuric acid is the oxidising agent, it must take electrons from something else and itself get reduced.

Here that means: $\text{X}^- \rightarrow \text{X}_2$ (oxidation) and $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{SO}_2$ (reduction).

**Test sodium chloride first**

With solid NaCl, concentrated sulfuric acid acts only as an acid, not as an oxidiser. You get white fumes and no redox.

$$\text{NaCl(s) + H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(l)} \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4\text{(s) + HCl(g)}$$

**Test sodium bromide and sodium iodide**

With NaBr and NaI, the HBr and HI first formed are strong enough reducing agents to reduce sulfuric acid. That is why you see coloured vapours.

$$\text{2HBr + H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + \text{2H}_2\text{O}$$
$$\text{2HI + H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + \text{2H}_2\text{O}$$
Iodide goes even further to S and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$.

**Conclude the pattern**

Chloride ion is too weak a reducing agent to reduce $\text{S(VI)}$ in sulfuric acid, but bromide and iodide can. So sulfuric acid oxidises bromide and iodide only.

options.A: Incorrect. Sodium chloride gives only HCl by acid-base reaction. Chloride cannot reduce concentrated H2SO4, so no oxidation by sulfuric acid occurs here.
options.B: Incorrect. While bromide is oxidised to Br2 with formation of SO2, chloride is not. This option wrongly includes sodium chloride where sulfuric acid acts only as an acid.
options.C: Correct. Both Br- and I- are strong enough reducing agents to reduce H2SO4 to SO2 (and for I-, further to S and H2S) while being oxidised to Br2 and I2. So sulfuric acid acts as an oxidising agent in both cases.
options.D: Incorrect. It is true for sodium iodide, where purple I2 fumes plus SO2, S and H2S are seen, but it misses sodium bromide which is also oxidised to brown Br2 fumes with SO2 formed.
